Global boundedness and asymptotic behavior of the chemotaxis system for Alopecia Areata with weakly singular sensitivity

Pengxue Xiang Affiliation:  School of Sciences, Shihezi University, Shihezi 832003, P.R. China    Yuebo Cao Affiliation:  School of Sciences, Shihezi University, Shihezi 832003, P.R. China    Hongying Yang ††thanks: Corresponding author: yanghongying2000@shzu.edu.cn. Affiliation:  School of Sciences, Shihezi University, Shihezi 832003, P.R. China

Abstract

This paper considers the homogeneous Neumann initial-boundary value problem for Alopecia Areata chemotaxis model with weakly singular sensitivity. For any appropriately regular initial conditions, it is shown that the problem admits a global boundedness of classical solutions in two spatial dimensions. Moreover, through the explicit construction of Lyapunov functions, we establish that the globally bounded solution converges exponentially to a constant steady state. The paper concludes with numerical experiments that serve to visually illustrate and corroborate some of the theoretically derived findings.

MSC: 92C17; 92C30; 35K65; 35B45; 35B40

Keywords: Chemotaxis; Alopecia areata; Weakly singular sensitivity; Boundedness; Asymptotic behavior

1 Introduction

Alopecia areata (AA) is a common non-scarring hair loss disorder, typically characterized by sudden patchy hair loss on the scalp in round or oval shapes. In severe cases, hair loss may involve the entire scalp or even the whole body. Although the disease is not life-threatening, it can easily lead to psychological issues such as image-related anxiety and depression. Its pathogenesis is complex, primarily involving the erroneous attack of hair follicles by T lymphocytes, which forces hair follicles into the telogen phase. This process involves the interaction among CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ\gamma). IFN-γ\gamma is secreted by both CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, diffuses and gradually attenuates in the body, while T cells exhibit both random and directed migration characteristics[3, 14]. In recent years, research on simulating the occurrence and development process of such types of alopecia using mathematical modeling methods has gradually drawn attention. Dobreva et al. [1] proposed

Currently, no research has been conducted on the system (1) with weakly singularity. To gain a better understanding of weakly singularity, we first review the classical Keller-Segel model with weakly singularity that is, χ⁡(v)=χvk\chi(v)=\frac{\chi}{v^{k}}, k∈(0,1)k\in(0,1), χ>0\chi>0, as exemplified by the following chemotaxis model

{ut=Δu−χ∇⋅(uvk∇v)+ru−μu2,x∈Ω,t>0,τ​vt=Δ​v−α​v+β​u,x∈Ω,t>0.\displaystyle{}\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}u_{t}=\Delta u-\chi\nabla\cdot(\frac{u}{v^{k}}\nabla v)+ru-\mu u^{2},&x\in\Omega,t>0,\\ \tau v_{t}=\Delta v-\alpha v+\beta u,&x\in\Omega,t>0.\end{array}\right.

When τ=0\tau=0 and n=2n=2, Zhao [34] proved that the system (1) has a globally bounded classical solution if μ\mu is suitably large, without establishing a uniformly positive lower bound for vv. when n≥3n\geq 3, Kurt [6] showed that the (1) has a globally bounded classical solution and this solution exponentially converges to the constant steady state (rμ,βα,rμ)(\frac{r}{\mu},\frac{\beta}{\alpha},\frac{r}{\mu}). Whenn≥2n\geq 2, he proved that the system (1) admits a globally uniformly bounded classical solution under the additional assumption k<12+1nk<\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{n} [7]. Later, Le and Kurt[12] established that the system possesses a globally bounded classical solution provided that μ\mu is sufficiently large, with the required threshold depending on the value of nn. When we consider that the system (1) is fully parabolic, that is, τ=1\tau=1 and n=2n=2, Le [9] proved that, by considering an energy function that allows the singularity of vv near zero to be incorporated into the diffusion effect, the system (1) admits uniformly bounded solutions. Subsequently, when μ\mu is sufficiently large, he demonstrated that the system (1) admits a unique nonnegative classical solution, which extends the previous boundedness result from n=2n=2 to n≥3n\geq 3[10].

In view of the aforementioned analysis of the classical Keller- Segel model with weakly singularity, in this paper, we consider the following model (1)

in a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} with a smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, where ν\nu denotes the outward unit normal vector to ∂Ω\partial\Omega. The parameters χi,μi​(i=1,2)\chi_{i},\,\mu_{i}\,(i=1,2), rr are positive and k∈(0,1)k\in(0,1). And the initial data (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) satisfies

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we present the local existence and uniqueness of solutions as well as some basic estimates. The first lemma, which states that there is the local existence and uniqueness of this classical solution, has a proof based on the standard contraction mapping argument and the fixed-point argument in Banach spaces.

Lemma 2.1.

[25, 4] Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a smoothly bounded domain. Assume that the functions χi>0\chi_{i}>0 (i=1,2)(i=1,2), and the nonnegative initial data (u0,v0,w0)(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}) satisfies (1). Then there exist Tmax∈(0,∞]T_{\text{max}}\in(0,\infty] and a uniquely determined triple (u,v,w)(u,v,w) of positive functions from C0​(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax))C^{0}(\bar{\Omega}\times[0,T_{\text{max}}))\cap C^{2,1}(\bar{\Omega}\times(0,T_{\text{max}})) solving (1) in Ω×(0,Tmax)\Omega\times(0,T_{\text{max}}). In addition,

eitherTmax=∞,orlimt↗Tmaxsup{‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)}=∞.\displaystyle\text{either}\quad T_{\text{max}}=\infty,\quad\text{or}\quad\lim_{t\nearrow T_{\text{max}}}\sup\left\{\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|v(\cdot,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\right\}=\infty.

From this point onward, we shall refer to (u,v,w)(u,v,w) as the distinct solution to the system (1) within the domain Ω×(0,Tmax)\Omega\times(0,T_{\text{max}}), where Tmax∈(0,∞]T_{\text{max}}\in(0,\infty], as confirmed by Lemma 2.1. The proof is grounded in the standard Lp−LqL^{p}-L^{q} estimates pertaining to the Neumann heat kernel; for an in-depth demonstration.

The following lemma, directly deduced from [27] [Corollary 1.2], presents a refined variant of the Gagliardo–Nirenberg interpolation inequality. This refined inequality will subsequently serve as a crucial tool for deriving LpL^{p} bounds for both uu and vv in Lemma 3.7. For the proof of this lemma, we refer to [11] [Lemma 2.6] and [Lemma 2.7].

Lemma 2.4.

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a bounded domain with a smooth boundary, and suppose m>0m>0 and γ>ξ≥0\gamma>\xi\geq 0. Then, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that the inequality

∫Ωϕm+1​lnξ⁡(ϕ+e)​𝑑x≤\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\phi^{m+1}\ln^{\xi}(\phi+e)\,dx\leq ε⁡(∫Ωϕ​lnγ⁡(ϕ+e)​𝑑x)​(∫Ω|∇ϕm2|2​𝑑x)\displaystyle\varepsilon\left(\int_{\Omega}\phi\ln^{\gamma}(\phi+e)\,dx\right)\left(\int_{\Omega}|\nabla\phi^{\frac{m}{2}}|^{2}\,dx\right)
+ε​(∫Ωϕ​𝑑x)m​(∫Ωϕ​lnγ⁡(ϕ+e)​𝑑x)+C\displaystyle+\varepsilon\left(\int_{\Omega}\phi\,dx\right)^{m}\left(\int_{\Omega}\phi\ln^{\gamma}(\phi+e)\,dx\right)+C

holds for any nonnegative function ϕ∈C1​(Ω)\phi\in C^{1}(\Omega).

Proof.

Since γ>ξ≥0\gamma>\xi\geq 0, one can verify that for any δ>0\delta>0, there exists c1>0c_{1}>0 such that for any a≥0a\geq 0 we have

am+1​lnξ⁡(a+e)≤δ​am+1​lnγ⁡(a+e)+c1.a^{m+1}\ln^{\xi}(a+e)\leq\delta a^{m+1}\ln^{\gamma}(a+e)+c_{1}.

This entails that

∫Ωϕm+1​lnξ⁡(ϕ+e)≤δ​∫Ωϕm+1​lnγ⁡(ϕ+e)+c1​|Ω|.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\phi^{m+1}\ln^{\xi}(\phi+e)\leq\delta\int_{\Omega}\phi^{m+1}\ln^{\gamma}(\phi+e)+c_{1}|\Omega|.

By applying Sobolev’s inequality when n=2n=2, there exists a positive constant c2c_{2} such that

∫Ωϕm+1​lnγ⁡(ϕ+e)≤c2​(∫Ω|∇(ϕm+12​lnγ2⁡(ϕ+e))|)2+c2​(∫Ωϕ​lnγm+1⁡(ϕ+e))m+1.\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}\phi^{m+1}\ln^{\gamma}(\phi+e)\leq c_{2}\left(\int_{\Omega}\left|\nabla\left(\phi^{\frac{m+1}{2}}\ln^{\frac{\gamma}{2}}(\phi+e)\right)\right|\right)^{2}+c_{2}\left(\int_{\Omega}\phi\ln^{\frac{\gamma}{m+1}}(\phi+e)\right)^{m+1}. (2.1)

By using elementary inequalities, one can verify that

|∇(ϕm+12​lnγ2⁡(ϕ+e))|≤c3​ϕ12​lnγ2⁡(ϕ+e)​|∇ϕm2|,\displaystyle\left|\nabla\left(\phi^{\frac{m+1}{2}}\ln^{\frac{\gamma}{2}}(\phi+e)\right)\right|\leq c_{3}\phi^{\frac{1}{2}}\ln^{\frac{\gamma}{2}}(\phi+e)|\nabla\phi^{\frac{m}{2}}|,

where c3=C⁡(m,γ)>0c_{3}=C(m,\gamma)>0. This, together with Hölder’s inequality leads to

c2​(∫Ω|∇(ϕm+12​lnγ2⁡(ϕ+e))|)2≤c4​∫Ω|∇ϕm2|2⋅∫Ωϕ​lnγ⁡(ϕ+e),\displaystyle c_{2}\left(\int_{\Omega}\left|\nabla\left(\phi^{\frac{m+1}{2}}\ln^{\frac{\gamma}{2}}(\phi+e)\right)\right|\right)^{2}\leq c_{4}\int_{\Omega}\left|\nabla\phi^{\frac{m}{2}}\right|^{2}\cdot\int_{\Omega}\phi\ln^{\gamma}(\phi+e), (2.2)

where c4=c2​c3c_{4}=c_{2}c_{3}. By Hölder’s inequality, we deduce that

c2​(∫Ωϕ​lnγm+1⁡(ϕ+e))m+1≤c2​(∫Ωϕ)m​(∫Ωϕ​lnγ⁡(ϕ+e)).\displaystyle c_{2}\left(\int_{\Omega}\phi\ln^{\frac{\gamma}{m+1}}(\phi+e)\right)^{m+1}\leq c_{2}\left(\int_{\Omega}\phi\right)^{m}\left(\int_{\Omega}\phi\ln^{\gamma}(\phi+e)\right). (2.3)

Collecting (2.1) - (2.3) implies that

∫Ωϕm+1​lnγ⁡(ϕ+e)≤C​∫Ω|∇ϕm2|2⋅∫Ωϕ​lnγ⁡(ϕ+e)+C​(∫Ωϕ)m​(∫Ωϕ​lnγ⁡(ϕ+e)).\int_{\Omega}\phi^{m+1}\ln^{\gamma}(\phi+e)\leq C\int_{\Omega}\left|\nabla\phi^{\frac{m}{2}}\right|^{2}\cdot\int_{\Omega}\phi\ln^{\gamma}(\phi+e)+C\left(\int_{\Omega}\phi\right)^{m}\left(\int_{\Omega}\phi\ln^{\gamma}(\phi+e)\right). (2.4)

Now for any fixed ε\varepsilon, we choose δ=εC\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{C} and apply (2.4) to have the desire inequality in this lemma. ∎

3 Global boundedness

In this section, we present several significant estimates for solutions, particularly deriving the L​ln⁡LL\ln L boundedness and LpL^{p} boundedness for uu and vv. And on this basis, we will prove Theorem 1.1. Let’s commence with an L1L^{1} bound as outlined in the following lemma:

Lemma 3.1.

∫Ωu⁡(⋅,t)≤M∫Ωv⁡(⋅,t)≤Mand∫Ωw⁡(⋅,t)≤Mfor all ​t∈(0,Tmax),\displaystyle{}\int_{\Omega}u(\cdot,t)\leq M\quad\int_{\Omega}v(\cdot,t)\leq M\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{\Omega}w(\cdot,t)\leq M\quad\text{for all }t\in(0,T_{\max}), (3.1)

∫tt+τ∫Ωu2≤Land∫tt+τ∫Ωv2≤Lfor all ​t∈(0,Tmax−τ),\displaystyle{}\int_{t}^{t+\tau}\int_{\Omega}u^{2}\leq L\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{t}^{t+\tau}\int_{\Omega}v^{2}\leq L\quad\text{for all }t\in(0,T_{\max}-\tau), (3.2)

τ:=min⁡{1,14​Tmax}.\tau:=\min\left\{1,\frac{1}{4}T_{\max}\right\}.

For any p≥1p\geq 1, there exists C>0C>0 such that

=−∫Ω|∇w|2+∫Ωu+∫Ωv≤2M.\displaystyle=-\int_{\Omega}|\nabla w|^{2}+\int_{\Omega}u+\int_{\Omega}v\leq 2M.

Therefore, applying Gronwall’s inequality to this implies that

∫Ωwp≤c1​(∫Ω|∇w|2​p2+p)p+22+c1​(∫Ωw)p≤c2for all ​t∈(0,Tmax),\int_{\Omega}w^{p}\leq c_{1}\left(\int_{\Omega}|\nabla w|^{\frac{2p}{2+p}}\right)^{\frac{p+2}{2}}+c_{1}\left(\int_{\Omega}w\right)^{p}\leq c_{2}\quad\text{for all }t\in(0,T_{\text{max}}),

where c1>0c_{1}>0 and c2>0c_{2}>0. The proof is now complete. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

There exists C>0C>0 such that

Proof.

Let y⁡(t):=∫Ωu⁡(⋅,t)​ln⁡u⁡(⋅,t)+∫Ωv⁡(⋅,t)​ln⁡v⁡(⋅,t)+12​∫Ω|∇w​(⋅,t)|2y(t):=\int_{\Omega}u(\cdot,t)\ln u(\cdot,t)+\int_{\Omega}v(\cdot,t)\ln v(\cdot,t)+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla w(\cdot,t)|^{2}. By differentiating the function with respect to time, we can acquire

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

By utilizing standard estimates pertaining to heat semigroups, we are now in a position to establish the uniform boundedness of solutions. We use a similar method in the proof of Theorem 0.1 in [25].

5 Numerical simulation

To reveal the spatiotemporal dynamics of the AA system (1), we illustrate some of our theoretical results by numerical calculations. To this end, we restrict ourselves to the two‑dimensional rectangular domain Ω=[0,2​π]×[0,2​π]\Omega=[0,2\pi]\times[0,2\pi] with a uniform Cartesian grid, following the idea of [30]. The spatial step sizes are taken as Δ​x=Δ​y=0.5\Delta x=\Delta y=0.5, yielding 13×1313\times 13 grid points. The spatial derivatives of system (1) are discretized using second‑order finite differences: the Laplacian is approximated by the standard five‑point stencil, while the chemotaxis term −∇⋅(uχ(w)∇w)-\nabla\cdot(u\chi(w)\nabla w) is treated by a finite‑volume method that first computes fluxes on cell faces and then assembles the divergence, thereby guaranteeing mass conservation. Neumann (zero‑flux) boundary conditions are imposed consistently for all variables.

Throughout our numerical experiments, we employ the explicit Euler method for time integration with a fixed time step Δ​t=0.01\Delta t=0.01, a value that satisfies the stability condition of the diffusive part. At each time step, we simultaneously update the three unknowns uu, vv and ww by evaluating all spatial operators (diffusion, chemotaxis, and reaction) from the current state. A positivity‑preserving cutoff max⁡(⋅,10−6)\max(\cdot,10^{-6}) is applied after each update to avoid non‑physical negative densities. The initial condition is a constant state (u0CLOSE(u_{0}, v0v_{0}, w0w_{0}) = (2.52.5, 2.52.5, 5.05.0) plus a small normally distributed perturbation 𝒩∼(0,0.22)\mathcal{N}\sim(0,0.2^{2}), which mimics a state far from the positive equilibrium. To monitor the spatio‑temporal evolution, we record the solution uu (since the distributions of the three variables are similar) at the four time instants t=10t=10, 2020, 6060, 10001000 and t=10t=10, 2020, 6060, 16001600. For visualization, a three‑dimensional surface plot is generated after a seven‑fold linear interpolation of the coarse grid data, while a global colormap is set by the 1st–99th percentiles of the first three snapshots to allow direct comparison between different times.

Case 1 : k=0.8k=0.8 μ1=0.8μ2=0.9r=0.1.\mu_{1}=0.8\quad\mu_{2}=0.9\quad r=0.1. Then u0=2.5v0=2.5w0=5.u_{0}=2.5\quad v_{0}=2.5\quad w_{0}=5.

Case 2 : k=1k=1  μ1=0.8μ2=0.9r=0.1.\mu_{1}=0.8\quad\mu_{2}=0.9\quad r=0.1. Then u0=2.5v0=2.5w0=5.u_{0}=2.5\quad v_{0}=2.5\quad w_{0}=5.

Considering a reaction-diffusion-coupling system, when initiated from initial random perturbations, its evolutionary process can be described through the following sequential stages: the waves diminish in intensity, followed by the merging of peaks and valleys, then a transition towards a quasi-uniform state, and finally the system attains an asymptotic steady state. Ultimately, the system trends towards a spatially uniform distribution (or an approximately planar distribution). At this stage, the combined net effects of reaction, diffusion, and coupling mechanisms equal zero, and the system achieves a homogeneous steady state. This behavior confirms the asymptotic stability of the system under specific parameter balancing and highlights the synergistic equilibrium between diffusion transport and nonlinear reaction. Furthermore, when the chemotaxis index 0<k<10<k<1, the convergence rate is significantly slowed down, and the system requires a longer time to reach the steady state.
